lines: Cold War territorial air defence combined warning networks,
interceptors and ground defences. Protecting national airspace
favours local readiness, at the expense of distant operations and
strategic bombing.
Wartime bomber commands and Cold War strategic forces organised
sustained attacks on infrastructure. Long campaigns need
considerable fuel and divert effort from defensive interception.
Korean War air-ground cooperation shaped later tactical air
commands. Close support aids the land battle, but sustained flying
consumes fuel and diverts air-superiority resources.
Cold War fighter commands sought control of contested airspace
through patrols, detection and escort. The commitment consumes
fuel and reduces the effort available for close air support.
Later unmanned air campaigns combined remote crews and
coordinated strike systems. Advanced control technology is
required; specialist staffing and prolonged qualification remain
costly.
Cold War medium-sized air forces maintained several roles within
limited fleets. Flexible commands support varied missions, but
broader qualifications demand more personnel and slower training
progression.
Cold War joint air planning coordinated fighters, attack aircraft and
support elements. Combined operations gain flexibility, but require
additional fuel and a substantial coordinating staff.
Swedish Bas 60 and Bas 90 dispersed aircraft and ground crews.
Mobile servicing and rapid repair sustain local defence, but duplicate
services cost more personnel and favour a shorter operating radius.
Dispersed Air
Defence
Finnish defensive priorities and North Vietnamese controlled attacks
conserved smaller fighter forces. Selected interceptions trade
sustained air-superiority patrols and distant escort for local
effectiveness.
Selective Air Denial
Israeli attacks in 1967 demonstrated rehearsed strikes against
enemy air bases. Coordinated packages improve attack preparation,
but consume more fuel and divert effort from home air defence.
Offensive Counter
Air
Argentine air attacks in 1982 threatened a stronger fleet. Maritime
search and concentrated strikes contest the sea approaches,
sacrificing close air support and broad air-superiority operations.
Maritime Air Denial
Portuguese African operations combined light aircraft with
dispersed ground support. Sustained tactical assistance suits limited
hostile air power, sacrificing fighter combat and strategic bombing.
Counterinsurgency
Air Support
Radar-led Cold War commands concentrated information and
assigned missions centrally. Coordination improves, but
administrative staff cost more and restricted local responsibility
slows operational learning.
Theatre and regional commands delegated authority to local air
leaders. Independent judgement preserves experience, but
duplicated support consumes more fuel and distant escort is harder
to coordinate.
Wartime carrier experience shaped Cold War naval aviation.
Fleet-directed aircraft concentrate on maritime operations, with
greater fuel demand and less attention to land close support.
Cold War fighter-bombers combined several missions in one aircraft
family. Versatile equipment reduces the need for separate designs,
but its compromises limit peak agility.
Cold War air forces also procured aircraft for distinct combat tasks.
Specialist performance improves, but maintaining separate fleets
requires more trained personnel.
Heavy Cold War aircraft carried large payloads, sensors and fuel
reserves. Endurance and specialist equipment come with higher
production cost and less agility.
Early unmanned reconnaissance led to later remotely piloted aircraft
designs. Lightweight construction limits production demands, but
protection remains weaker even after refinement.
Late Cold War low-observable development prioritised concealment
and survivability. Suitable technology is required; specialised
construction costs more and configuration compromises reduce
range.
Vietnam-era and later electronic support aircraft collected signals
and assisted strike packages. Specialist crews cost more, while
electronic equipment competes with offensive weapon employment.
Cold War equipment commonality and later modular systems
simplified support and adaptation. Flexible interfaces aid service,
but cost coordinating personnel and limit peak attack performance.
Second World War bomber commands evolved into Cold War
strategic forces. Long-range bombing needs fuel and disciplined
crews, while heavy aircraft retain limited agility.
Cold War maritime patrol aircraft combined long endurance with
specialised sensors and weapons. Patrol formations gain maritime
capability, but their configurations reduce agility.
Vietnam-era gunships provided sustained fire where enemy air power
was limited. Specialist crews improve support, but slow aircraft
remain vulnerable in contested airspace.
Cold War airborne warning extended surveillance and battle
management beyond ground radar. Control networks aid other
formations, but large support aircraft consume fuel and specialist
personnel.
Berlin and subsequent Cold War deployments demonstrated the
value of strategic airlift. Long routes and sustained schedules
require fuel and a substantial support establishment.
Cold War tankers extended the practical reach of combat aircraft.
Better procedures improve coordination, but tanker sorties still
increase total fuel demand and personnel costs.
Cold War multirole squadrons shared aircraft across several tasks.
Balanced capability avoids a single narrow mission, but broader
qualifications cost personnel and slow training progression.
Cold War fighter-bombers concentrated on carrying weapons to
tactical targets. Attack proficiency improves, but loaded
configurations sacrifice agility.
Cold War commands integrated fighter-bombers into varied air
missions. Flexible packages combine capabilities, but their
equipment and preparation limit range and require additional staff.
Later Cold War multirole fighters could concentrate on air combat
when required. Fighter employment improves at the expense of
ground-attack and bombing proficiency.
Cold War carrier aircraft combined fleet defence and attack roles.
Flexible deck operations require costly crews and longer
qualification before those skills can be used effectively.
Korean and Vietnam War experience shaped dedicated close-support
aircraft. Ground-attack configurations support troops, but sacrifice
range and air-to-air performance.
Cold War naval strike crews trained for navigation, search and
maritime weapon release. Specialist personnel cost more, while
attack configurations reduce aircraft agility.
Late Cold War precision and support arrangements improved attack
preparation. Specialist arming personnel cost more, and complex
weapon preparation reduces mission efficiency.
Vietnam-era defence-suppression training and later coordinated
packages addressed increasingly complex threats. Specialist
preparation improves strike survivability, but costs staff and diverts
ground firepower.
Cold War interdiction planning sought targets beyond the immediate
battle. Deep missions consume fuel and draw aircraft away from
close support of troops at the front.
Cold War air campaigns attempted to disrupt movement and
reinforcement over time. Sustained attack schedules require more
fuel and a permanent planning staff.
Light Cold War fighters offered relatively economical air combat and
local readiness. Their size limits operating radius and protection
even when crews become proficient.
Dedicated Cold War fighters prioritised detection, combat and
escort. Specialised airframes deliver strong air-to-air performance,
but cost more industrial production.
Cold War radar and missile training developed beyond-visual-range
engagements. Suitable aircraft and weapons remain necessary;
radar-centred employment trades agility and specialist staffing for
detection and attack.
Vietnam-era experience renewed close-combat instruction for
fighter crews. Manoeuvre and mutual awareness improve, but
qualification progresses more slowly and the chosen profiles favour
shorter range.
Late Cold War low-observable work informed later fighter
employment. Concealment requires appropriate technology and
costly specialist support, while restrictive configurations limit
attack flexibility.
Cold War interceptors defended threatened sectors through
controlled scrambles. Strong interception sacrifices prolonged
air-superiority patrols and distant escort commitments.
Long-endurance reconnaissance preceded operational armed MALE
campaigns after the Cold War. Advanced drone systems are required;
vulnerable platforms still need a substantial control staff.
Carrier UCAS programmes developed after the Cold War. Advanced
unmanned systems and an actual carrier are required; deck
qualification and remote control demand more personnel and
training.
Later unmanned strike systems combined expendable aircraft with
target preparation. Suitable technology is required; compact
platforms trade range and control personnel for the chosen attack
role.
Cold War point defence addressed small and low-flying threats
before later drone-specific systems. Local warning and interception
protect installations, but require staff and divert distant escort
effort.
Large coordinated unmanned formations are a post-Cold-War
capability. Advanced control and expendable-aircraft technology are
required; vulnerable platforms and difficult coordination remain
constraints.
Swedish dispersed-base practice sent servicing crews beyond main
airfields. Mobile teams restore operations, but duplicated services
need more personnel and complicate distant escort commitments.
Dispersed Servicing
Teams
Aggressor training and Red Flag from 1975 confronted crews with
unfamiliar threats. Combat preparation preserves experience, but
maintaining realistic exercises requires more fuel and instructor
staff.
Adversary Air
Training
Cold War Swedish requirements favoured dispersed operation and
simple servicing. Maintainable tactical airframes reduce accidents,
production and staff costs, accepting a modest speed limitation.
Field Maintainable
Designs
Light attack aircraft supported troops in Korea and the Portuguese
African wars. Robust platforms favour ground fire and recoverability
at the expense of speed and air-to-air performance.
Rugged Attack
Designs
Berlin in 1948 and 1949 demonstrated disciplined airlift schedules and
maintenance. Specialist transport crews improve reach and delivery,
but require more personnel and slower qualification.
Tactical Airlift
Procedures
Norwegian Orion operations from 1969 emphasised maritime and
underwater search. Specialist crews exploit fitted sensors over wide
approaches, accepting less strike emphasis and higher personnel
costs.
Maritime Search
Coordination
RAF Tornado attacks in 1991 exposed both the purpose and risks of
low-level penetration. Fast strike profiles improve survivability, but
reduce range and bombing performance while raising accident risk.
Low Level
Penetration
Late Cold War strike packages combined designation, specialist
support and suitable weapons. Deliberate attacks gain reach and
accuracy, but cost more personnel and divert immediate
close-support effort.
Stand Off Strike
Packages
Korean War airborne controllers and ground liaison teams
coordinated attacks near friendly troops. Better control
strengthens close support, requiring specialist staff and diverting
strategic bombing effort.
Forward Air Control
Argentine pilots in 1982 attacked ships at very low altitude with
bombs and missiles. Concentrated low approaches threaten fleets,
but sacrifice operating radius and increase the risks of flight.
Sea Skimming Strike
Finnish defensive choices and North Vietnamese ground control
favoured selected opportunities. Fighters improve brief interception
engagements, accepting weaker continuous patrols and distant
escort.
Ambush
Interception
Section tactics such as the Thach Weave in 1942 protected weaker
fighters through teamwork. Mutual cover preserves formations and
escorts, trading individual attack freedom and ace generation for
discipline.
Section Mutual
Support
Ryan drones in Vietnam and later Israeli RPVs collected intelligence
before modern armed UAV campaigns. Control and exploitation
teams support reconnaissance, but need specialist staff and
vulnerable platforms.
Reconnaissance
RPV Operations
Israeli RPVs in 1982 gathered intelligence and acted as decoys
alongside strike aircraft. Coordinated support improves target
preparation and survivability, but exposes unmanned platforms and
requires control staff.
Decoy RPV
Operations
